definition.text: Average cost, or unit cost, is total cost divided by the number of units produced.

facts.text: It is an important factor in how businesses decide what price to charge.
A typical short-run average cost curve is U-shaped: fixed costs are spread over more units at first, then rising marginal costs from diminishing returns push it up.
When marginal cost is below average cost, average cost falls; when above, it rises; the rising marginal cost curve crosses average cost at its lowest point.
A factory built for a set output has high average cost below it from idle equipment and above it from bottlenecks.
Average fixed cost keeps falling toward zero as output grows, and the gap between average cost and average variable cost equals average fixed cost.
With high fixed costs and constant marginal cost, as in hydroelectric generation, average cost slopes down continuously toward marginal cost.
Productive efficiency means goods are supplied at the lowest possible average total cost.

definition.text: The unit cost of producing a given output when every input, including buildings and machinery, can be changed.

facts.text: The firm is assumed to pick the cheapest mix of inputs for each output level.
The curve is most often U-shaped, sloping down where there are economies of scale and up where there are diseconomies of scale.
If input prices do not change with the firm's purchases, economies of scale arise exactly when the production function has increasing returns to scale.
Under perfect competition, long-run equilibrium has every firm producing at the lowest point of this curve.
Where it keeps falling indefinitely, the biggest firm has a cost advantage and the industry tends to become a natural monopoly, as in water and electricity supply.

definition.text: A group of independent firms that agree not to compete with each other so as to raise their profits and dominate a market.

facts.text: Cartels fix and raise prices by creating artificial shortages through low production quotas, stockpiling and marketing quotas.
They are inherently unstable because each member is tempted to cheat, selling below the agreed price or above its quota.
Outsiders often respond to the shortage by producing more, using the good more efficiently or investing in substitutes.
A survey of studies found the median cartel price increase over the last 200 years was about 23 percent, 28 percent for international and 18 percent for domestic cartels.
Discovered 20th-century cartels lasted on average 5 to 8 years.
The US Sherman Act of 1890 was the first enforced law against cartels; price fixing is now illegal in more than 140 countries.
Oligopolies may form cartels; OPEC is one of the best-known international cartels.
Adam Smith argued cartels were undesirable because they could limit production and the quality of goods.

definition.text: An economic model of an oligopoly in which firms compete by each choosing, at the same time, how much to produce.

facts.text: Firms sell an identical product, each firm's output affects the price, and each seeks the most profit given rivals' output.
Each firm takes rivals' quantities as given, looks at the demand left over, and acts like a monopolist on it.
The price settles where demand equals the total quantity all firms produce.
Antoine Augustin Cournot set it out in 1838 to describe a spring-water market with two suppliers.
Its equilibrium, where no firm wants to change output, was the first use of what is now called a Nash equilibrium.
Prices are lower and quantities higher under duopoly than under monopoly.
As the number of firms grows the price keeps falling, approaching marginal cost when firms are infinitely many.
Joseph Bertrand criticised it, arguing that rivals would instead undercut each other's prices.

definition.text: The cost advantages a business gains from operating on a larger scale, so that each unit of output costs less.

facts.text: They occur when average costs fall as output increases.
Common sources are bulk buying, specialised managers, cheaper borrowing, spreading advertising costs and returns to scale in production.
Some have a physical basis: by the square–cube law a vessel's surface grows with the square of its size but its volume with the cube.
A rough engineering rule says capital cost changes with the 0.6 power of the capacity ratio.
They help explain why firms grow large in some industries and patterns in international trade.
Economies of scale concern a firm's costs, while returns to scale describe how outputs respond to inputs in the production function.
Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) gave the first systematic analysis, through the division of labour.
Economies of scale and learning-by-doing can lower the costs of climate technologies over time.

title: External economies of scale
article: Economies of scale#External economies of scale

definition.text: Cost savings that come from the growth of a whole industry and benefit most or all of its firms, not just one.

facts.text: They tend to be more common than internal economies of scale.
The entry of new firms lowers average cost for all firms, while internal economies help only the single firm.
Sraffa argued such economies are rarely met with and that, under perfect competition, economies of scale should be excluded.

title: Learning and growth economies
article: Economies of scale#Learning and growth economies

definition.text: Dynamic economies of scale that come from the process of growing and from experience, rather than from size itself.

facts.text: Learning by doing improves skills and brings small innovations that steadily lower average costs.
Learning economies rise with cumulative production, the experience curve.
Growth economies arise when expanding lets a firm use resources or skills it had not fully used.

title: Cournot's dilemma
article: Economies of scale#Economies of scale and the tendency towards monopoly: "Cournot's dilemma"

definition.text: The puzzle that strong economies of scale should logically lead to monopoly, yet many industries keep numerous firms of different sizes.

facts.text: Marshall noted Cournot's premises implied the first firm to get a good start would monopolise its trade, and named factors such as founders' deaths that limit this.
Morroni argues that once knowledge and the organisation of transactions are included, economies of scale do not always lead to monopoly.

definition.text: A business cost, also called overhead, that does not change with how much the business produces.

facts.text: Fixed costs tend to recur, like monthly rent or interest, and are often capital costs.
For a bakery, rent and the phone line are fixed costs, while wages are variable because more output needs more workers.
They are fixed only for a period by contract, and in the long run there are no fixed costs because all inputs can change.
Fixed costs act as an entry barrier for new businesses.
Some costs are mixed or semi-variable, such as a phone bill with a fixed charge plus calls.
Accounting and economics use the terms differently, and in recent years fixed costs have come to exceed variable costs at many companies.

definition.text: A curve joining all the combinations of two or more inputs that produce the same quantity of output.

facts.text: Its axes are two inputs such as labour and capital, and it is a level set of the production function.
It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, but output on it can be measured exactly in physical units.
Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the rate at which one input can replace the other; because this diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin.
Perfect-substitute inputs give straight isoquants; perfect complements give L-shaped ones with a kink at the fixed ratio.
The least-cost input mix is where an isoquant touches an isocost line, so the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices.
On an isoquant map, isoquants spreading further apart as output rises signal decreasing returns to scale, and closer together increasing returns.
Two isoquants can never cross.

definition.text: In economics the short run is a period when some inputs or prices cannot yet change, while the long run is long enough for everything to adjust fully.

facts.text: In microeconomics the long run has no fixed inputs, so firms can change their capital or enter and leave industries; in the short run some inputs are fixed.
In macroeconomics the long run is when prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted.
Alfred Marshall introduced the distinction in his 1890 Principles of Economics; there is no hard rule for how long each period is.
In the long run firms enter, exit or resize their plants in response to profits and losses, moving toward minimum long-run average cost.
All actual production happens in the short run, where only variable inputs such as labour and raw materials can change output.
In the short run a profit-maximising firm expands output while marginal cost is below marginal revenue and cuts it when above.
Keynes criticised neglect of the short run with the remark 'In the long run, we are all dead'.

title: Marginal product

definition.text: The extra output gained by using one more unit of an input, such as one more worker, while other inputs stay the same.

facts.text: With divisible inputs it is the derivative of the production function with respect to that input.
As more of one input is added to a fixed amount of another, marginal product first rises, then falls, and can finally turn negative.
When total product reaches its maximum, marginal product is zero.
The marginal product of labour is the slope of the total product curve.
In neoclassical theory of competitive markets the marginal product of labour equals the real wage.
Output is usually measured ignoring external costs and benefits.
The Cambridge capital controversy showed the claim that capital's marginal product equals its return cannot generally hold in multi-good models.

contested_note: The Cambridge capital controversy disputed whether the marginal product of capital equals its rate of return outside one-good models.

definition.text: A market with many producers selling products that are differentiated, for example by brand or quality, so they are not perfect substitutes.

facts.text: Textbook examples include restaurants, cereals, clothing, shoes and city service industries.
Products differ in real or perceived ways such as style, reputation or location, but remain close substitutes.
Each firm has a little market power, facing a downward-sloping demand curve, so it can raise its price without losing all customers.
Entry and exit are free, so economic profit can be positive in the short run but approaches zero in the long run.
It is inefficient: firms charge more than marginal cost and operate with excess capacity, below the output of minimum average cost.
Product variety can raise total utility by better meeting people's wants, while heavy advertising is a common concern.
Edward Chamberlin pioneered the theory in his 1933 book, alongside Joan Robinson's work on imperfect competition.

title: Production function

definition.text: A technical relation showing how much output can be made from given quantities of physical inputs.

facts.text: It is usually taken to give the maximum output obtainable from each combination of inputs, so it traces a frontier.
It links physical inputs to physical outputs; prices and costs are not part of it.
Written Q = f(X1, ..., Xn), its inputs are factors such as capital, labour, land or raw materials, and no inputs means no output.
It is used to define marginal product and to study allocative efficiency.
A production function homogeneous of degree above 1 shows increasing returns to scale, below 1 decreasing, and exactly 1 constant returns.
In macroeconomics, aggregate production functions split growth into the part from more capital and the part from better technology.
The Cobb–Douglas form, first developed in 1927, was the first aggregate production function to be estimated and presented to economists.
Some economists reject aggregate production functions, and a 1950s-1970s debate begun by Joan Robinson questioned how capital is measured.

contested_note: Economists have long debated whether aggregate production functions and the measurement of capital in them are valid.

title: Natural resources in production functions

definition.text: The debate over how, or whether, standard production functions should include natural resources such as energy.

facts.text: Natural resources are usually left out of production functions.
Solow and Stiglitz added natural resources in a way that let man-made capital fully substitute for them.
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called this a 'conjuring trick' because it ignored the laws of thermodynamics; neither Solow nor Stiglitz replied.
Treating energy as an independent input gives a form like Q = A L^β K^α E^χ, which later work says misrepresents how energy affects production.
An alternative makes labour and capital themselves depend on energy, Q = f(L(E), K(E)).
If a region cannot get the resources needed to build or maintain machines, their output eventually falls to near zero.

contested_note: Georgescu-Roegen disputed Solow and Stiglitz's assumption that man-made capital can fully substitute for natural resources.

definition.text: The three ranges into which a production function is divided according to how output per unit of the variable input changes.

facts.text: In stage 1 output per unit of the variable input rises to a peak, so a price-taking firm always produces beyond it.
In stage 2 output still rises but at a decreasing rate, with average and marginal product both falling.

definition.text: The process by which a firm chooses the price, inputs and output that give it the highest possible total profit.

facts.text: Mainstream economics assumes the firm is a rational agent that wants to maximise profit, total revenue minus total cost.
Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit; marginal cost is the extra cost of making it.
Profit is highest where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; if marginal revenue is larger, producing more adds profit.
Under perfect competition the firm's demand curve is its marginal revenue curve, a horizontal line at the market price.
In the short run a change in fixed costs does not change the profit-maximising output or price, because fixed costs are treated as sunk.
Where extra customers cost almost nothing, such as seats on a scheduled flight, maximising profit means maximising revenue.
Some profit-maximising behaviour harms consumers and is regulated by competition law.
Behavioural economics replaces strict profit maximisation with bounded rationality in its models.

title: Marginal revenue product rule
article: Profit maximization#Marginal product of labor, marginal revenue product of labor, and profit maximization

definition.text: The rule that a firm maximises profit by using more of an input until the extra revenue it brings equals the input's extra cost.

facts.text: For labour the rule is MRP_L = MC_L.
The marginal revenue product is the change in total revenue per unit change in the input.

definition.text: How much a firm's output rises, in proportion, when it increases all its inputs together in the long run.

facts.text: Constant returns: doubling all inputs doubles output; decreasing returns: output less than doubles; increasing returns: output more than doubles.
Decreasing returns come mainly from harder management and coordination as scale grows; increasing returns from efficiency gains of larger scale.
A firm may have increasing returns at low output, constant in between and decreasing at high output.
In mainstream theory returns to scale are set purely by technology, not by market conditions.
With fixed input prices, constant, decreasing and increasing returns mean constant, rising and falling long-run average costs.
For a Cobb–Douglas function, returns are increasing if the exponents sum to more than 1, constant if 1, and decreasing if less.
Path-dependent increasing returns to scale help lock industrial economies into fossil-fuel energy systems.

definition.text: The overall process of inventing, innovating and spreading new technologies or processes.

facts.text: It covers invention, commercialisation, research and development, continual improvement and diffusion through industry or society.
The old linear model of innovation has largely given way to one with innovation at every stage of research, development, diffusion and use.
Improvement is often modelled as a learning curve of falling costs, as with fuel cells becoming cheaper every year.
Models such as climate models once treated it as external but now more often treat it as something policy can influence.
In economics it is a change in the set of feasible production possibilities.
In market economies profit is a powerful driver, so technologies that meet social needs but promise little profit may never reach market.
By the Jevons paradox, efficiency improvements can raise rather than lower total use of a resource.

definition.text: The hypothesis that policymakers can steer the direction of technical progress by changing relative input prices.

facts.text: Climate policy that makes fossil energy relatively more expensive is the standard example.
Empirical evidence that policy induces innovation is still lacking, partly because of long-term policy uncertainty.
The related idea of directed technical change stresses price-driven direction rather than policy-driven scale.

definition.text: The spread of a technology through a society or industry.

facts.text: Adoption usually follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first, then rapid, then levelling off as the market saturates.
Everett Rogers named five attributes that speed acceptance: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, trialability and observability.
Mass media mostly build awareness, while face-to-face contact mostly reduces the uncertainty that blocks adoption.

definition.text: Ways of classifying technical progress by which input's productivity it raises.

facts.text: Hicks-neutral change, after John Hicks (1932), leaves the ratio of capital's and labour's marginal products unchanged at a given capital-labour ratio.
Harrod-neutral change is labour-augmenting and Solow-neutral change is capital-augmenting.

definition.text: A set of economic theories that explain and predict the nature of firms such as businesses and corporations.

facts.text: The nature of the firm covers its origin, survival, behaviour, structure and relation to the market.
It asks why not every transaction goes through the market, and where the boundary between firm and market lies.
Around the First World War economists shifted from industry-level to firm-level analysis as perfect competition no longer described how firms behaved.
Its main frameworks include transaction cost theory, managerial economics, behavioural theory, the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities.
Managerial theories by Baumol, Marris and Williamson suggest managers pursue their own utility, for example maximising sales once profit satisfies shareholders.
Agency theory explains the governance problems that come from separating ownership and control.

title: Transaction cost theory of the firm
article: Theory of the firm#Transaction cost theory

definition.text: Ronald Coase's explanation that firms exist because organising some production inside a firm costs less than coordinating it through market exchange.

facts.text: Coase set out the theory in his 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm', one of the first attempts to define the firm in relation to the market.
It explains the firm in a way consistent with constant returns to scale rather than relying on increasing returns.
Coase asked why all production is not carried on by one big firm, the starting point for the economics of outsourcing.
Later economists note the line between within-firm and between-firm transactions is blurred by intermediate forms such as inter-firm cooperation.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm

title: Behavioural theory of the firm

definition.text: An approach, developed by Cyert and March, that explains how decisions are actually made inside firms, going beyond neoclassical economics.

facts.text: It builds on Herbert Simon's idea that limited cognitive ability allows only bounded rationality in complex, uncertain situations.
People and groups therefore 'satisfice', aiming for realistic goals rather than maximum utility or profit.
The neoclassical theory of the firm was not seriously challenged by managerial and behavioural alternatives until the 1960s.

distinct_from: Transaction cost theory of the firm
Property rights theory of the firm

title: Asset specificity

definition.text: Oliver Williamson's idea that firms exist because some assets are tied to each other and worth much less in any other use.

facts.text: If such assets are owned by different firms, the parties get locked in and bargain at length over the gains from trade.
Repeated or long transactions need renegotiation, raising transaction costs further.

distinct_from: Transaction cost theory of the firm
Property rights theory of the firm

title: Resource-based view of the firm
article: Theory of the firm#The resource-based and knowledge-based theories

definition.text: The view that a firm's lasting competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.

facts.text: It grew from Edith Penrose's 1959 argument that a firm is a collection of productive resources whose growth depends on managers finding new uses for idle ones.
Wernerfelt (1984) and Barney (1991) developed the resource-based view.

distinct_from: Transaction cost theory of the firm
Property rights theory of the firm

title: Property rights theory of the firm

definition.text: The approach of Grossman, Hart and Moore that explains firm boundaries through ownership of assets when contracts are incomplete.

facts.text: In modern contract theory the theory of the firm is often identified with this property rights approach.
Its seminal works, Grossman and Hart (1986), Hart and Moore (1990) and Hart (1995), built the incomplete contracting paradigm.
Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment and so invests too little, the hold-up problem.
The approach explains the pros and cons of merging firms and has also been applied to public good provision and privatization.

distinct_from: Transaction cost theory of the firm

definition.text: A cost that changes as the quantity a business produces changes.

facts.text: Variable costs equal the sum of marginal costs over all units produced; with fixed costs they make up total cost.
Common examples are sales commission, labour and raw materials, such as the cloth and labour in each shirt a clothing maker produces.
Some costs are semi-variable, like electricity with a fixed standing charge plus a usage charge.
Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on the time horizon: over five years all costs can become variable.
Not all variable costs are direct costs; variable manufacturing overhead is indirect.

definition.text: The short-run rule that a firm should keep producing as long as its revenue covers its variable costs, and shut down if it does not.

facts.text: A firm earning more than variable cost but less than total cost keeps operating while making an economic loss.
In the short run fixed costs are paid even at zero output, so they do not affect the decision.
